1.why: Both /api/verify-token and /api/reset-password enforce token.sessionId === session.id and a matching account hash, so the reset code is verified as belonging to the requesting session/user.

2.why: Each token is bound to the originating sessionId and marked single-use, so the same code cannot be redeemed by any other session or user.

3.why: No session-invalidation logic runs on password reset; the resetting session continues into MFA and any other sessions in the map remain valid until their 30-minute expiry.

4.why: The app serves HTTPS with TLS cert/key, sets HSTS, and 308-redirects HTTP to HTTPS, but the TLS version is not pinned in code so 'latest' cannot be confirmed.

5.why: Reset codes are stored only as SHA-256 hashes and passwords are bcrypt-hashed (appropriate one-way protection rather than reversible encryption), and no other user data is persisted.

6.why: The simulated delivery message contains only the recovery code and same-origin link and is returned solely to the requesting browser session, exposing no other private user data.

7.why: All inputs pass strict allow-list regex and length checks (validIdentifier/validToken/validMfa), JSON content-type is required, and the DOM is updated only via textContent.

8.why: The only redirect is a hardcoded same-origin 308 to the HTTPS listener, the verification link is same-origin, and CSP locks form-action and base-uri to 'self'/'none'.

9.why: The mock email is plain text rendered through textContent with no user input rendered as HTML, and nonce-based CSP blocks untrusted scripts.

10.why: Error responses are generic, but the recovery token and full verification link are deliberately written to the browser console and the in-page 'Logs' panel, so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and reset tokens stored as SHA-256 hashes, but the MFA security code is hardcoded in source as MOCK_MFA_CODE = "482916".

12.why: No default accounts or credentials exist and passwords are user-set under a strong policy, though the demo's fixed MFA code is a shared known value.

13.why: Server-side per-address throttling caps recovery requests at 3 per 10 minutes and token and MFA failures at 5 per 10 minutes, returning 429 beyond those limits.

14.why: recovery-request always returns the same generic 'If the details match an account…' message and issues a mock token for any well-formed identifier, so account existence is never revealed.

15.why: The code is a 256-bit randomBytes value, single-use with a 10-minute TTL and bound to the session and account hash, though the mock maps all users to one shared mock account.
